<details>
This PKGBUILD is a standard, checksum-pinned build of Tencent QQ for Linux. The `package()` function only installs into `$pkgdir`, fixes the `.desktop` file, copies license files, and removes macOS `.dylib` leftovers — ordinary packaging steps.

The most notable element is the custom `DLAGENTS` entry that invokes the local `linuxqq-get-url.sh` helper for https downloads. This is explained in the maintainer comment as required because QQ's CDN only accepts URLs signed via `im.qq.com`'s GetSign endpoint — a known constraint for QQ packages. The helper is a local file shipped in the same AUR repo (listed in the `source` array), not something fetched at build time from an external host, and the artifact it downloads still goes through makepkg's normal output path and is verified against the pinned b2sums. The main caveat is that the helper script itself and the referenced `linuxqq-nt.install` are not visible in this file, so a complete audit should review them as well — but nothing in this PKGBUILD indicates exfiltration, obfuscation, code injection, or execution of untrusted content.

Two things are worth noting as packaging considerations rather than threats: `chmod 4755` makes `chrome-sandbox` a setuid-root helper (a deliberate, widely used Electron sandboxing approach, though a known privilege-escalation surface), and the package installs a prebuilt upstream binary that runs with the user's privileges. Neither matches the defined indicators of a supply-chain attack.

<details>
This is a conventional wrapper script for launching the QQ desktop application. It performs three basic tasks: (1) cleans the contents of the application's own crash-report directory under `~/.config/QQ/`, (2) reads optional user-supplied command-line flags from `qq-flags.conf`, and (3) uses `exec` to launch the real binary at `/opt/QQ/qq` with those flags. Nothing in the script touches files outside the application's own config scope, and there are no network operations, downloads, or code execution from external sources.

The `rm -rf -- "$CRASH_DIR"/*` is properly guarded: the `--` prevents option injection, the `! -L` check prevents following a symlinked crash directory, and deleting crash dumps in `~/.config/QQ/crash_files` is a routine, privacy-positive cleanup of the app's own diagnostic files. The flags-file loop trims whitespace, skips comments/blank lines, and appends entries to an array that is later expanded with full quoting, so lines from the config file are treated as data (flags), never re-parsed as shell syntax. There is no obfuscation, no suspicious host access, and no behavior outside the normal purpose of an Arch Linux application launcher wrapper.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>

Only standard tools (bash, curl, python3) are used, all appropriate for the task.

The dynamic link-signing behavior means the downloaded artifact is ultimately served from a URL produced by Tencent's server. This is the script's intended function and represents the same trust model as downloading a vendor package normally, not a supply-chain attack by the AUR maintainer. Any remaining notes are minor hygiene considerations (e.g., relying on python3/curl being installed at build time) and do not rise to the level of a security threat.
